data.title: History
data.headline: It started with a milk cart.
data.excerpt: A farm on Elm Street. An ice cream stand in 1939. The stand you know today.

children.text: In the 1920s, Charles Hayward wasn’t satisfied working for the Whiting dairy. He bought a few cows of his own, pushed a milk cart around Milford, and saved enough to buy the old Smith Farm on Elm Street. His three sons helped turn one cart into milk routes across southern New Hampshire.
Summer 1939

His son Stanley built the family’s roadside ice cream stand in 1939. It opened that summer with 18 flavors and sold 11,000 gallons before the season was out, according to Milford History Online. The town’s 1942 tax list records six acres of the Smith farm and an ice cream stand.

A second stand opened in Nashua in June 1940, the year printed on Hayward’s cups. The postcard above calls the Milford stand “the original Hayward Farms Stand,” the place where ice cream for all the others was made.
In the yearbooks

By 1948 the stand had added a self-service frozen food store with 192 items, and Hayward Farms was advertising in the Milford High School yearbook. A year later, the yearbook described its seniors in riddles. Two of them shared a clue: “Works at Hayward’s.” One of the two, it added, liked blond wavy hair and maroon Ford coupes.

content.alt: Color postcard of the same stand with a green roof, an orange car out front and “Frozen Foods” on the Hayward Farms sign
content.caption: An undated postcard. The back offers steaks, vegetables and “even a frosted stuffed lobster.” Boston Public Library, Tichnor Brothers Collection.

children.text: The town’s 1965 report thanks Hayward Farms for Christmas ice cream, enough for every elementary pupil.
Back on Elm Street
Fires and deaths in the family slowed the old company, and in time the farm closed. The stand you see today was built in 2001, on land that was once part of Hayward Farms.

content.alt: The white Hayward’s stand on Elm Street today, with its curved roof and red sign
content.caption: The stand on Elm Street today.

children.text: For years the ice cream itself was made elsewhere, from Hayward’s recipes. In January 2008, ice cream making started up again in Milford. Hayward’s joined the New Hampshire Ice Cream Trail in 2022.
Still in the family

Sharon Robinson runs the stand on Elm Street today, and the ice cream in the case is made right here. Chris Ordway runs Hayward’s in Nashua, and Dianne O’Donnell runs Hayward’s in Merrimack. Mike Ordway runs Mike’s Ice Cream in Dracut, Massachusetts.

All four are grandchildren of Charles P. and Fredericka Hayward, who opened the Nashua stand in 1940, and great-grandchildren of Charles A. Hayward, the man with the milk cart. Every one of them kept ice cream in the family.

We follow
New Hampshire’s youth employment law

. If you’re under 16, you’ll need a youth employment certificate, which your school or a parent can give you, and the law limits when and how long you can work. If you’re 16 or 17, a parent or guardian signs a permission form, unless you’ve finished high school.

data.title: Milkshake vs. frappe: what’s the difference?
data.excerpt: You may already know if you grew up in New England. If you didn’t, here’s why there are two lines on our menu.

children.text: Every summer someone steps up to the window, reads the menu twice and asks: what’s the difference between a milkshake and a frappe? It’s a fair question. Most of the country would tell you there isn’t one.
Around here, there is

In New England, a milkshake is the old-fashioned kind: milk and flavored syrup, blended until it’s frothy. No ice cream. Order one expecting something thick and you might get a lesson in regional vocabulary instead.
A frappe has ice cream, milk and syrup, blended thick. It’s what most of the country would call a milkshake. Around here it’s usually said “frap,” with a quiet e.
And then there’s Rhode Island

In parts of Rhode Island and southeastern Massachusetts, the same drink is a cabinet, usually coffee-flavored. The story goes that it’s named for the cabinet the blender was kept in. We don’t make the rules.
So which one do you want?
We have both on the menu. If you want it thick, get a frappe. Choose regular or extra thick. If you’re not sure which you’re after, ask at the window.
Aimee Tucker,
“The Difference Between a Milkshake and a Frappe,”
Yankee Magazine, 2022: milkshakes, frappes and cabinets
“frappe,” Dictionary.com
: said “frap,” chiefly in eastern New England
